description: We’re here to participate in the hackathon, have a fun time, and learn more about space while building something interesting. Our skills include programming, AI/ML, web development, and problem-solving, and we’re excited to apply them to a real-world space challenge.
summary: LunaNav is a browser based lunar landing site navigator for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. At the lunar south pole the Sun barely rises, so small relief casts long shadows, and Earth can sit behind terrain that a flat-horizon model ignores. LunaNav asks that question directly: is the Sun actually above this site's skyline, and is Earth? Choose one of three published candidates (Shackleton Rim, Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache Rim) or click anywhere on the polar map, set a landing date and mission length, then read terrain-adjusted Sun and Earth elevation, clearance, visibility intervals, blackouts and mission metrics. Compare two scenarios, see what a ten-day launch slip changes, apply your own requirements, and inspect mapped PSRs without being told there is water ice. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, the skyline from LRO LOLA elevation models (5 m per pixel near each site, 80 m out to 150 km), the maps from Moon Trek imagery. Missing data is shown as missing. A solar-powered polar lander needs both light and a line to Earth, and the two don't often peak together.
details: As LunaNav is a browser tool for picking a landing site near the lunar south pole, the Sun never climbs far above the horizon. A crater rim a few kilometres away can hide it for days, and Earth can sit behind terrain a flat-horizon model ignores. So the skyline is the main object here, not a correction. Choose one of three published candidates (Shackleton Rim, Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache Rim) or click the polar map, set a landing date and mission length, and the app shows when the Sun and Earth are actually above the terrain: elevation, skyline angle, clearance, intervals and blackouts. Scenarios can compare side by side, and a date can move. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons for each site's own observer: 1,014 hourly records, agreeing with an independent model to 0.032°. LRO LOLA terrain, 5 m per pixel near each site and 80 m out to 150 km, is ray-marched into that skyline. Moving de Gerlache from 1 to 11 December lifts Earth visibility from 2.3 hours to 4 days 5 hours and cuts the blackout from 6 d 22 h to 2 d 19 h, though the 12-hour requirement still fails. Impact matters here: a planner gets reproducible metrics and a report, a student a plain-language view, and water ice stays "not assessed". It runs on FastAPI, NumPy, React, TypeScript, Leaflet, Recharts and Three.js, with pytest, Vitest and Playwright tests. The creative choice was making the horizon the interface, and letting the decision view say "no eligible site".
